strengths: The central algorithmic contribution is well-motivated: Gibbs et al. [2023]'s RKHS-based conditional conformal prediction is theoretically appealing but computationally prohibitive, and the proposed (λ,S)-path algorithms address a genuine bottleneck by tracing piecewise-affine solution paths at the cost of inverting only small elbow-set matrices rather than refitting the full regression. The derivations (Appendices B.2–B.4) are complete and careful, with KKT-based event tracking, closed-form initialization, and updates for both paths.

The theoretical section is a genuine extension rather than a restatement: Lemma 4 adapts the randomized coverage result of Gibbs et al. to the optimal λ̂-defined RKHS class with an explicit monotonicity proof (Proposition 3), Theorem 1 quantifies a measurable coverage gap under kernel reweighting in the latent space, Theorem 2 handles exchangeable-but-dependent admixture data that violates the i.i.d. assumption of the prior work, and Lemma 10 bounds how embedding estimation error propagates into the conditional guarantee.

Empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: synthetic admixture with covariate shift, three molecular graph benchmarks, arXiv abstracts, and brain tumor MRI, with sensible baselines (CondCP, SplitCP, PCP, RLCP), repeated subsampling (50 runs), and detailed appendix materials including cutoff statistics that transparently show instability of competing methods.
Reproducibility is treated seriously: a Python package is provided with code to reproduce all experiments, and Appendix D.3 documents hardware, solvers, and environment.
The limitations section is honest and specific (fixed α, unweighted quantile loss, scalar regression focus), and the authors correctly do not overclaim exact conditional coverage.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely incremental relative to prior work. The path-following technique directly builds on Li et al. [2007] (RKHS quantile regression solution paths) and Takeuchi et al. [2006] (α-path), and the coverage framework is inherited from Gibbs et al. [2023]; the novelty lies in the S-path for the imputed test score, the joint (γ,λ) tuning, and the latent-space extension. This is useful but not a fundamentally new method.

The theory provides approximate, not exact, conditional coverage. The gap term in Theorem 1/Lemma 4 (−λ̂E⟨ĝ,fψ⟩) is inherited from Gibbs et al. and the reweighting interpretation (conditioning on W′ drawn from the kernel) is a somewhat indirect relaxation; Theorem 2 additionally requires the strong alignment condition T̂(X)=T(X) a.s. (Assumption 11) plus a margin condition, so the cleanest guarantee applies only in restrictive regimes.

Some empirical results are less convincing than the headline claims: Table 2 shows SpeedCP at 0.730±0.34 coverage on the ML topic (well below nominal with high variance), and SpeedCP remains orders of magnitude slower than SplitCP (e.g., 31s vs <0.01s), so the '40-fold speedup' holds only relative to CondCP. The 30% interval-length improvement is also not uniformly demonstrated across all benchmarks.

Presentation has notable flaws: the abstract's phrase 'finite-sample conditional guarantees' overstates what is proved (approximate conditional guarantees); the package URL is missing on page 3; Remark 5 references a 'SIC criterion' never defined in the manuscript; and there are typos (e.g., 'intervel'). These are fixable but detract from polish.

Conditional coverage is evaluated on partitions (10 simplex bins, Voronoi cells on 3-8 PCs) that are chosen by the authors; sensitivity of conclusions to the partitioning scheme is not systematically explored, and some experiments (e.g., MRI with PCA rank 8, Table 6) show smaller differences between methods than the main table suggests.

The cross-validation step for (γ,λ) uses a fixed grid for γ and k-fold splits of the calibration set, but there is no discussion of the computational cost of this tuning loop (λ-path per fold per γ) relative to the reported per-test-point times.

strengths: The core algorithmic contribution is real: tracing the full solution path of the regularized RKHS conformal quantile problem (λ-path for smoothness, S-path for the score cutoff) removes the prohibitively expensive binary-search-over-refits of Gibbs et al. [2023], and the derivations in Appendix B (KKT-based elbow/left/right set tracking, piecewise-affine segment laws, explicit update formulas and initialization) are careful and largely self-contained.
The empirical speedup over CondCP is substantial and clearly documented (e.g., Table 1: ~30s vs ~600–1900s), and the paper is honest that this is the comparison that motivates the work.

The extension to low-rank latent embeddings with a kernel defined on π̂(X) is a sensible way to handle p ≫ n, and the coverage analysis (Lemma 4, Theorem 1, Theorem 2 for admixture/exchangeable latent-variable settings, embedding-error perturbation results in Lemmas 7–10) goes beyond a trivial adaptation by relaxing i.i.d. to exchangeability and quantifying the effect of estimating π̂.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: a Python package, code for all experiments, hyperparameter/protocol details (folds, splits, Voronoi partitions, computation environment), and an explicit limitations section.
Experiments span four reasonably diverse settings (synthetic admixture, molecular graphs, arXiv topics, MRI images) with several relevant baselines (SplitCP, CondCP, PCP, RLCP).
weaknesses: The contribution is largely incremental relative to existing work: the λ-path is a direct adaptation of the RKHS quantile regression solution path of Li et al. [2007] and Takeuchi et al. [2006], and the S-path mirrors the construction of Gibbs et al. [2023]; the theoretical guarantees (Lemma 4, Proposition 3) are explicitly re-derivations of Gibbs et al.'s Theorem 3/4 with modest changes. The novelty lies mainly in engineering and the latent-space wrapper.

The headline claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The '30% interval-length improvement' and '40-fold speedup' hold only against CondCP; against SplitCP — the actual default method — SpeedCP's interval sizes are essentially identical (Table 1: 1.135 vs 1.122 on QM9; 1.789 vs 1.800 on ESOL) while being 10^3–10^4× slower, and marginal miscoverage is comparable (Table 4: 0.105 vs 0.107). The added value over SplitCP is only the (approximate) conditional coverage story.

The conditional coverage achieved is not uniformly reliable even on the paper's own terms: on the ArXiv data (Table 2), SpeedCP attains 0.730 ± 0.34 on the ML topic against a 0.9 target — a serious undercoverage with huge variance — and its advantage over SplitCP on other topics is marginal, whereas RLCP achieves near-nominal coverage everywhere at the cost of wider sets. This undercuts the central claim of 'reliable conditional coverage across a variety of settings.'

The theoretical target itself is weakened: Theorem 1 conditions on W′ drawn from the kernel at π̂(Xn+1), a kernel-reweighted relaxation whose gap term is not distribution-free and depends on unknown expectations; the 'measurable gap' is only bounded under additional strong convexity and moment assumptions (Assumptions 3–4). Meanwhile the hyperparameters (γ, λ̂) are selected by k-fold cross-validation on the very calibration scores later used for conformal calibration, a circularity whose effect on the finite-sample guarantees is not analyzed.

Several citation and consistency errors undermine polish: PCP is attributed to [Meng, 1994] on page 7 (it is Zhang and Candès [2024]); RLCP is attributed to both [Guan, 2023] (LCP) and [Hore and Barber, 2023] interchangeably; typos such as 'intervel', 'principle components'; Proposition 1's statement (affine in λ vs affine in 1/λ) is inconsistent between the main text and the proof.

Scalability and practicality are not convincingly established: the S-path must be run per test point, worst-case cost is O((n+d)^3), the claimed practical advantage rests on the unproven assertion that |E| ≪ n, and no experiment demonstrates behavior as n grows. Runtime comparisons against SplitCP/RLCP (both orders of magnitude faster with adequate marginal validity) are not discussed in the main text.

Evaluation of conditional coverage relies on post-hoc partitioning (kmeans/Voronoi bins) whose sensitivity to the partition choice is not assessed, and several key empirical claims (uniform coverage in Figure 1, 'CondCP fails to attain reasonable coverage') are difficult to verify from the presented figures.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: Gibbs et al. (2023)'s RKHS-based conditional conformal prediction (CondCP) has strong theoretical promise but prohibitive computational cost (binary search over imputed scores with a fresh RKHS fit per candidate). The proposed (λ, S)-path algorithms replace the binary search with piecewise-affine path tracing, which is a clean and effective way to make this family of methods deployable.

The algorithmic development is technically careful: KKT-based elbow/left/right set characterization, closed-form piecewise-affine representations (Propositions 1-2), monotonicity of the test-point coefficient in the imputed score (Proposition 3), explicit update rules, and honest worst-case complexity analysis (O((n+d)^3) worst case, |E| << n in practice). Full derivations are provided in Appendices B.2-B.4.

Experiments are unusually broad for this area: a controlled synthetic admixture setting with covariate shift, three molecular graph benchmarks (QM9, QM7b, ESOL), ArXiv topic-conditional intervals, and a CNN-based MRI task, with multiple baselines (CondCP, SplitCP, PCP, RLCP) and joint reporting of coverage, set size, and runtime, aggregated over 50 repetitions.

The theory contribution extends Gibbs et al.'s guarantees in two meaningful directions: relaxations from i.i.d. to exchangeability (Assumption 1) and to conditioning on estimated low-rank embeddings, with a perturbation analysis quantifying how embedding error (π̂ vs π) degrades the guarantee (Lemmas 7-10). Theorem 2 handles latent-variable/exchangeable (non-i.i.d.) structures not covered by prior work.
Reproducibility is good: a Python package (speedcp), code to reproduce experiments, hyperparameter grids, data splits, and computing environment details (Appendix D.3) are all provided.
The limitations section is candid, discussing fixed α, unweighted quantile loss, and the need for further study of Φ* choices; this honesty should not be penalized.
weaknesses: Overstated framing of the guarantees. The abstract claims 'finite-sample conditional guarantees,' but the actual results (Theorem 1, Lemma 4) deliver only a kernel-reweighted relaxation of conditional coverage, with a coverage gap that is 'measurable' but not shown to be small under verifiable conditions. The paper should state upfront that exact conditional validity remains impossible (as the authors themselves note via Barber et al.) and that SpeedCP provides approximate/reweighted coverage.

Limited methodological novelty beyond adaptation. The λ-path is a direct adaptation of existing RKHS quantile regression solution paths (Takeuchi et al. 2006; Li et al. 2007) to a setting with an added linear term, and the conformal wrapper follows Gibbs et al. (2023). The S-path is the most novel algorithmic piece, but overall the contribution is incremental relative to these known building blocks.

The theoretical assumptions are sometimes strong and their practical implications under-discussed: Theorem 2 requires T̂(X) = T(X) a.s. (exact top-topic alignment), which is a stringent requirement in real topic-model applications; Assumption 3-4 (population strong convexity, bounded moments) are stronger than the corresponding conditions in Gibbs et al. Also, Theorem 1 switches to an i.i.d. assumption that is stronger than the exchangeability touted in Assumption 1, creating some tension in the narrative.

Interplay between hyperparameter selection and validity deserves more scrutiny: (γ̂, λ̂) are chosen by k-fold CV on the same calibration data later used for conformal calibration. The authors assert this is acceptable because parameters are fixed before set construction, and Remark 5 addresses fixed λ in the S-path, but a formal statement (or at least discussion) of why data-dependent λ̂ does not invalidate the exchangeability-based guarantee would strengthen the paper.

Absolute computational cost remains high. The advertised 40-50x speedup is relative to CondCP only; SplitCP and RLCP are orders of magnitude faster (e.g., <0.01s vs ~31s per QM9 run; ~244s per MRI trial). For the MRI case CondCP had to be excluded entirely due to non-convergence, so the practical scope of the RKHS-class benefit is narrower than the speedup headline suggests.

Some empirical results are mixed or ambiguous: on ArXiv, SpeedCP's topic-wise coverage is nearly identical to SplitCP (e.g., 0.880 vs 0.877 on Geometry) with undercoverage on ML (0.730) and a substantially larger size (15.84 vs 15.66); the benefits over cheap baselines in real-data settings are therefore less compelling than in the synthetic setting. Minor presentational issues (e.g., inconsistent attribution of RLCP to Guan 2023 vs Hore and Barber 2023, several typos in equations and appendix derivations, mislabeled set L(S^l) in the Proposition 2 proof) suggest the manuscript needed one more careful pass.

The dependence on the quality of the low-rank embedding π̂ is central to performance but is explored only descriptively; there is no sensitivity analysis of how mis-specified K or degraded embeddings trade off coverage vs. set size, despite this being acknowledged as challenge (3) in Appendix A.2.
